target_domain: Data-driven plastic waste management, especially online characterization, sorting, and material-flow decision support for mixed, post-consumer plastic streams.
core_gap: Existing NIR/MIR spectroscopy, machine-learning classification, and early sensor-fusion sorting systems cannot yet provide robust, generalizable, uncertainty-aware, economically deployable characterization of dirty, aged, contaminated, pigmented, multilayer, and #3–#7 plastic waste under industrial conditions, nor reliably connect item-level material-state recognition to material-flow analysis, recycling yield, and circular-economy decisions.
objects: contaminants, residues, labels, inks, additives, and pigments
economic feasibility and environmental impact metrics
policy interventions such as bottle recycling, bag bans, and waste-to-fuel use
relations: spectral signatures are used to infer polymer identity, contamination, and material condition
contamination, aging, additives, and surface degradation reduce sorting confidence and recyclability
sensor fusion combines complementary modalities to improve discrimination of hard-to-sort plastics
material-state classification drives sorting, recovery, downcycling, or diversion decisions
item-level characterization should aggregate into reliable material-flow data
material flow analysis informs economically feasible and environmentally advantageous waste-management interventions
throughput, cost, and facility constraints limit the deployment of sensing and AI models
bottlenecks: spectral signal distortion caused by contamination, aging, pigments, moisture, labels, inks, fillers, and multilayer structures
poor generalization of trained models across waste streams, facilities, instruments, and geographic contexts
limited calibration transfer, domain adaptation, and uncertainty quantification in sorting systems
difficulty of identifying and separating low-value, heterogeneous #3–#7 plastics and multilayer packaging
need for high-throughput, low-cost, low-maintenance operation in real recycling facilities
disconnect between sensor-level classification and broader material-flow, economic, and policy decision-making
unresolved_tensions: high classification accuracy versus high-speed, low-cost industrial operation
rich multimodal sensing versus hardware affordability and maintenance burden
polymer identification versus assessment of material condition and recyclability
local waste-stream specificity versus globally transferable models
detailed material characterization versus actionable material-flow aggregation
desired_solution_properties: robust to dirty, aged, contaminated, pigmented, multilayer, and additive-laden plastics
operable online or inline with minimal sample preparation
capable of uncertainty estimation and confidence-aware sorting decisions
generalizable across instruments, facilities, waste streams, and geographic contexts
economically viable for high-throughput recycling operations
able to handle difficult #3–#7 plastics, mixed polymers, and low-value streams
able to connect material-state recognition with material flow analysis, recycling yield, and circular-economy decisions
supportive of policy and operational interventions such as bottle recycling, bag reduction, and waste-to-fuel pathways
possible_mechanism_types: multimodal sensor fusion with confidence-aware decision making

physics-informed or chemically informed spectral interpretation

decision-theoretic routing under cost, speed, and hardware constraints
integration of sensor telemetry with material-flow accounting
